sentence: Prostate cancer is a cancer that starts in the prostate, a small gland in the male reproductive system that sits just below the bladder.
note: Anatomy of the prostate is textbook-level (not re-retrieved in second pass).

sentence: Prostate cancer often causes no symptoms at first.
note: NHS symptoms page: often no symptoms at first.

sentence: When symptoms appear they are usually changes to passing urine.
note: NHS symptoms page: symptoms are usually urinary (trouble starting, weak flow, urgency, night-time).

sentence: The NHS says it often grows slowly and may never cause problems, so treatment is not always needed.
note: NHS treatment page: treatment is not always necessary; often grows slowly and may never cause problems.

sentence: Age, Black ethnicity and family history are linked with a higher risk.
note: Macmillan and Prostate Cancer UK both list age, ethnicity (Black men higher risk) and family history.

sentence: The NHS PSA test page says there is no national screening programme, and the UK National Screening Committee has recommended targeted screening for some men with a BRCA2 gene change.
note: NHS PSA page: currently no national programme; UK NSC final recommendation: targeted screening, BRCA2 variant plus family history.

sentence: The causes of prostate cancer are largely unknown, according to NHS 111 Wales
note: NHS 111 Wales: causes largely unknown; obesity and diet are areas of research.

sentence: Inherited changes in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes can raise the risk, according to Prostate Cancer UK
note: PCUK: BRCA1/BRCA2 changes can increase risk of breast, ovarian, pancreatic and prostate cancer but do not guarantee cancer.

sentence: Increasing age
note: Macmillan: uncommon before 50, more common over 75; PCUK: mainly men over 50.

sentence: Being from a Black ethnic background
note: Macmillan: Black men have a much higher risk and tend to develop it younger; PCUK: higher risk.

sentence: A father or brother who has had prostate cancer, with the risk greater if the relative was diagnosed at a younger age
note: Macmillan (under 65) and PCUK (under 60) differ on the age, so only "younger age" is stated.

note: Macmillan lists family history of breast or ovarian cancer.

sentence: A weak urine flow
Needing to pass urine urgently, often or during the night

sentence: Unexplained weight loss in advanced disease
Spread of the cancer beyond the prostate, which may need chemotherapy
note: NHS treatment page: if the cancer has spread, chemotherapy may be needed.

sentence: Lower back pain and unexplained weight loss in advanced disease

Hormone therapy side effects such as hot flushes, tiredness and weight gain
The NHS 111 Wales page lists blood tests, a digital rectal examination, an MRI scan and a biopsy as the most commonly used tests for prostate cancer.
note: NHS 111 Wales wording; NHS diagnosis page covers the same tests.

sentence: If a person is referred to a specialist because prostate cancer is possible, the NHS says an MRI scan is arranged.
A biopsy may follow, in which a small needle is put into the prostate to take a tissue sample to be checked for cancer cells.
If cancer is found, the NHS lists a CT scan, MRI scan, PET scan and bone scan as further tests that help decide on treatment.
note: NHS tests and next steps page lists these.

sentence: The NHS says treatment is not always necessary, and that for early cancer without symptoms it can be delayed until symptoms appear.
When treatment is needed it may include surgery, radiotherapy and hormone therapy, with chemotherapy if the cancer has spread.
Macmillan describes active surveillance as monitoring the cancer with regular PSA blood tests and MRI scans, with a biopsy usually only if there are signs the cancer may be growing.
note: Macmillan monitoring page: regular PSA tests, MRI at start and later, biopsy usually only if signs of growth.

sentence: The NHS says hormone therapy on its own does not cure prostate cancer but can slow it down and help with symptoms.
The Surrey and Sussex Cancer Alliance says prostate cancer is not linked to any clear preventable causes.

The NHS says there is currently no national screening programme for prostate cancer, and the UK National Screening Committee has recommended targeted screening only for some men with a BRCA2 gene change and a family history of cancer.
The NHS lists seeing a GP as non-urgent advice if a person has trouble passing urine or other symptoms of prostate cancer, or is worried about their risk.
note: NHS symptoms page: non-urgent advice, see a GP. No urgent route (999, NHS 111) was found on the page; none is invented.

sentence: Many of these symptoms have other causes, such as an enlarged prostate, so they do not by themselves mean a person has prostate cancer.
note: NHS symptoms page: enlarged prostate is a very common non-cancerous cause.

sentence: The NHS says prostate cancer often causes no symptoms at first.
When symptoms do appear, they are usually changes to passing urine.
The NHS lists difficulty starting to pass urine, a weak flow, needing to go urgently or often, and getting up to pass urine during the night.
Erection problems and blood in the urine or semen are also listed.
note: NHS symptoms page lists erectile dysfunction and blood in urine or semen.

sentence: In more advanced cases, the NHS lists lower back pain and unexplained weight loss.
Many of these symptoms can have other causes.
The NHS describes an enlarged prostate as a very common non-cancerous condition that becomes more likely as men get older and can cause similar urinary symptoms.
note: NHS symptoms page: enlarged prostate very common, caused by prostate getting larger with age.

sentence: The NHS lists seeing a GP as non-urgent advice if a person has trouble passing urine or other symptoms of prostate cancer, or is worried about their risk of prostate cancer.
note: NHS symptoms page: 'Non-urgent advice: See a GP if...'.

sentence: NHS 111 Wales says the causes of prostate cancer are largely unknown.
Macmillan says prostate cancer is uncommon before the age of 50 and more common over the age of 75.
Prostate Cancer UK says the condition mainly affects men over 50, and that the most common age at diagnosis is between 70 and 74.
Macmillan says Black men have a much higher risk of prostate cancer and tend to develop it at a younger age.
Prostate Cancer UK says about 1 in 4 Black men in the UK will get prostate cancer in their lifetime.
note: PCUK search summary (its infographic gives about 1 in 8 for men overall).

sentence: Macmillan lists a father or brother who has had prostate cancer as a risk factor, with a greater risk if the relative was diagnosed at a younger age.
note: Macmillan under 65; PCUK under 60; the exact age is therefore left out.

sentence: Prostate Cancer UK says a man is two and a half times more likely to get prostate cancer if his father or brother has had it.
Macmillan also lists a family history of breast or ovarian cancer.
Prostate Cancer UK says changes in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes can raise the risk of prostate cancer but do not guarantee it, and that such changes are uncommon.
The NHS PSA test page says there is currently no national screening programme for prostate cancer in the UK, because the PSA test is not always accurate.
It says routine PSA testing is not currently offered on the NHS unless genetic tests have shown a faulty version of the BRCA2 gene.
The UK National Screening Committee has made a final recommendation for targeted screening.
note: UK NSC page and CRUK news (May 2026).

sentence: It recommends PSA testing every 2 years for men aged 45 to 61 who have a BRCA2 variant that can cause disease and a family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer.
note: UK NSC page wording as returned in search.

sentence: It did not recommend screening the whole population or men with a family history but no BRCA2 variant, and it says it is still uncertain whether screening would do more good than harm for Black men.
A government equality impact assessment says ministers in England have agreed to a nationally managed approach to PSA testing every 2 years for this group.
Prostate Cancer UK cautions that it could take years for the programme to reach every eligible man.
note: PCUK caution as returned in search summary; start date not stated in sources.

sentence: The NHS says a raised PSA level may be a sign of prostate cancer but can also be caused by another condition, such as an enlarged prostate, prostatitis or a urinary tract infection, so a high result does not mean a person has cancer.
A 2016 Public Health England blog on GP guidance says a man aged 50 or over without symptoms can make an appointment with his GP to discuss PSA testing.
note: Search summary of the Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme guidance; dated 2016, so flagged as older.

sentence: NHS 111 Wales lists blood tests, a digital rectal examination, an MRI scan and a biopsy as the most commonly used tests for prostate cancer.
A digital rectal examination is a physical examination of the prostate, and the Royal Marsden says it cannot diagnose cancer on its own.
note: NHS diagnosis page names the exam as a physical examination of the prostate; Royal Marsden: cannot diagnose on its own.

sentence: The NHS says a GP assesses the chance of prostate cancer using factors such as PSA levels, the prostate examination, age, family history and ethnic group, and can refer a person to hospital for further tests.
If a person is referred to a specialist because prostate cancer is possible, the NHS says an MRI scan is arranged, which gives a clearer view of the prostate and shows whether more tests are needed.
If more information is needed, a biopsy may be suggested, in which a small needle is put into the prostate to take a tissue sample to be checked for cancer cells.
If cancer is found, the NHS lists a CT scan, MRI scan, PET scan and bone scan as further tests that help the team decide on treatment.
The NHS says it can take a few weeks to get test results.
note: NHS tests and next steps (search summary).

sentence: The NHS says treatment is not always necessary, and that for early cancer without symptoms it can be delayed until symptoms appear.
It also says prostate cancer often grows slowly and may never cause problems.
When treatment is needed it may include surgery, radiotherapy and hormone therapy, and chemotherapy may be needed if the cancer has spread.
Macmillan describes active surveillance as monitoring the cancer with regular tests instead of treating it straight away.
It involves regular PSA blood tests and MRI scans, and a biopsy is usually only needed if there are signs the cancer may be growing.
Macmillan says this avoids or delays the side effects of surgery or radiotherapy, and that treatment is offered if the cancer grows more quickly or symptoms develop.
The NHS says radiotherapy uses high-energy radiation to kill cancer cells.
Brachytherapy is a form of internal radiotherapy in which radiation is placed in the prostate.
note: Macmillan brachytherapy page title 'Internal radiotherapy'; Royal Marsden: internal radiation placed in the prostate.

sentence: The NHS says hormone therapy on its own does not cure prostate cancer but can slow it down and help with symptoms.
St George's University Hospitals says chemotherapy does not get rid of prostate cancer but aims to shrink it and slow its growth.
Macmillan says radiotherapy for prostate cancer can cause urinary and bowel irritation and problems getting or keeping an erection.
Cancer Research UK lists problems with erections, bowels or passing urine among the long-term effects of external radiotherapy.

Macmillan says brachytherapy causes similar side effects, and that on its own it is less likely than external radiotherapy to cause late bowel effects, although short-term urinary effects may be more severe.
Hormone therapy has its own side effects.
Macmillan lists tiredness, difficulty sleeping, hot flushes and weight gain, and St George's adds loss of sex drive, erection problems and breast swelling or tenderness.
Prostate Cancer UK says hormone therapy can weaken the bones.
note: PCUK external beam radiotherapy side effects page (search summary).

sentence: Royal Free London says these effects usually go away when treatment stops.
NHS 111 Wales advises that people with side effects from treatment should be referred to specialist services, such as continence services.
The NHS PSA test page says there is currently no national screening programme for prostate cancer, and routine PSA testing is not offered unless genetic tests have shown a faulty BRCA2 gene.

The UK National Screening Committee has recommended targeted screening for men aged 45 to 61 with a BRCA2 variant and a family history of certain cancers, and ministers in England have agreed to a nationally managed approach.
